quickStart: If anyone is in immediate danger or has a life-threatening emergency, call 999 or 112. Give the operator the exact location and postcode.
For urgent medical advice that is not a life-threatening emergency, use NHS 111 or the relevant NHS service for the nation; service routes differ across Great Britain.
Locate the exported ZIP and extract it to a private, secure folder. Keep an untouched copy of the original export.
Start with emergency contacts, health information, legal document locations, insurance, bank accounts, pensions, and essential bills.
Do not use another person's bank cards, online banking, passwords, or devices without the proper authority. Contact the relevant provider and follow its bereavement process.
Share the pack only with trusted people who need it. Keep passwords, PINs, one-time codes, and recovery keys out of the exported files.

emergencyServices.police: 999 or 112 for an emergency; 101 for non-emergency police contact in England, Wales, and Scotland
emergencyServices.urgent_health_advice: 111; use the appropriate NHS 111 / NHS 24 service for your nation

Personal Details.description: Identity and contact information used to match records and support family, medical, financial, and official processes.
firstActions: Confirm spelling and date of birth against official records
Keep the National Insurance number and NHS number in a secure place
Check that the address, email, and phone number are current

Emergency contact details.description: Trusted people to contact and the roles they may hold. Being listed here does not itself grant legal authority.
firstActions: Contact the person identified for the relevant situation
Check that contact details are current
Confirm that named attorneys or executors have copies of the formal documents

Health and Care Information.description: Health information, GP details, allergies, medication, and locations of care documents.
firstActions: Call 999 for a life-threatening emergency
Share known allergies and current medication with clinicians
Locate any formal advance decision, advance care plan, or power of attorney

Insurance policies.description: Private, employer, home, motor, and other insurance cover and the information needed to find policy terms.
firstActions: Locate the current policy schedule and claims contact
Check policy status, beneficiaries, exclusions, and claim requirements with the insurer
Do not assume NHS coverage is the same as private insurance

Bank accounts.description: Current and savings account references to help identify providers and ownership arrangements.
firstActions: Confirm account ownership and any joint-holder arrangements with the bank
Ask the bank about its bereavement process before attempting changes
Keep recent statements and account references available

Savings and investments.description: ISAs, NS&I products, investments, and other assets held with financial providers.
firstActions: Check ownership and beneficiary or nomination records
Request current valuations from providers
Do not sell or transfer assets until the authorised representative has checked the relevant rules

Pensions.description: State, workplace, personal, and public service pension records and provider contacts.
firstActions: Contact each scheme to confirm benefits, options, and claim steps
Check any expression-of-wish or beneficiary nomination with the scheme
Use GOV.UK's Pension Tracing Service if a provider is unknown; it finds contact details, not pension values

Property.description: Property addresses, ownership, mortgage, title, and insurance records.
firstActions: Locate title and mortgage documents
Confirm the registered ownership and any mortgage with the relevant organisations
Get jurisdiction-specific advice before transferring or selling property

Loans and liabilities.description: Debts and recurring liabilities, including any joint borrower or guarantor responsibilities.
firstActions: Contact creditors using their bereavement or account-support process
Check who is contractually responsible before making payments
Keep a record of balances, correspondence, and decisions

Employment, income and benefits.description: Employer, income, and benefit details that may help identify ongoing household support or survivor benefits.
firstActions: Contact the employer or benefit administrator to confirm entitlements and next steps
Check whether any benefit or pension must be notified separately
Keep recent payslips, P60s, and award letters

Tax and government records.description: HMRC, council, student loan, and government account references; authentication secrets must never be stored here.
firstActions: Use official GOV.UK services and verify current requirements
Keep tax records and correspondence for the authorised representative
Never share Government Gateway passwords or one-time codes

Legal and estate planning.description: Wills, powers of attorney, advance decisions, and appointed representatives. Rules and document names differ within Great Britain.
firstActions: Find the original or registered document and confirm its jurisdiction
For England and Wales, check whether an LPA is registered before an attorney acts
For Scotland, follow Scottish power-of-attorney and estate procedures; get local legal advice

Important documents location.description: An index of where official records and original documents are stored.
firstActions: Secure originals and tell the appropriate representative where they are
Check that the current version of each document is recorded
Do not put original identity or financial documents in an unsecured shared location

Digital accounts and devices.description: An inventory and recovery plan for digital services and devices. This section intentionally excludes passwords and authentication secrets.
firstActions: Use the provider's official legacy or bereavement process
Use password-manager emergency access rather than placing credentials in this export
Secure devices and recovery methods; do not bypass access controls

Additional details.description: Other practical notes that do not fit another section. Do not place passwords or access codes here.
firstActions: Check whether a note points to a formal document or professional contact
Keep information current and limit access to trusted people

legalNotes: This guide is general information, not legal, tax, insurance, or financial advice. Rules depend on the facts and the relevant UK jurisdiction.
Great Britain means England, Scotland, and Wales; Northern Ireland is not covered by this GB configuration and has separate processes.
Probate in England and Wales and confirmation in Scotland are not interchangeable. Scotland has distinct succession, estate, and power-of-attorney rules; obtain advice for the relevant jurisdiction.

In England, Scotland, and Wales, GOV.UK says Tell Us Once may be available after registration or qualifying coroner certification. Northern Ireland and people permanently living abroad are excluded; check current eligibility and use any reference within its stated validity period.
Tell Us Once does not notify every private organisation. Banks, mortgage providers, insurers, employers, and many personal or workplace pension schemes may still need to be contacted directly.
Do not distribute an estate, assume a particular account passes automatically, or pay another person's debts without confirming authority, ownership, and applicable law.
Official guidance: What to do when someone dies: https://www.gov.uk/when-someone-dies
Official guidance: Applying for probate in England and Wales: https://www.gov.uk/applying-for-probate
Official guidance: Making a will: https://www.gov.uk/make-will
Official guidance: Managing a lasting power of attorney: https://www.gov.uk/manage-lasting-power-attorney

fileStructure: The export is packaged as a ZIP containing the available spreadsheet, PDF, and this access guide.
Treat the files as highly sensitive: they may contain identity, account, health, and legal-record references.
Keep an untouched backup and note when the information was last reviewed.
dataAccess: Windows: right-click the ZIP file and choose Extract All. On macOS, double-click the ZIP file.
Store extracted files in an encrypted, access-controlled location and share only with trusted representatives.
Use an established password manager's emergency-access or legacy feature for credentials; do not add passwords or recovery codes to this export.
If a person has died, contact each financial and service provider and follow its bereavement process. A family relationship alone does not grant account access.
securityTips: Never store passwords, PINs, card security codes, one-time codes, or account recovery keys in this file or its export.
Use encrypted storage and a separate secure channel when sharing sensitive documents.
Enable multi-factor authentication and keep recovery methods current.
Make sure a trusted person knows where the encrypted record is kept and how to reach its authorised access method.
Review the record after major life events and at least annually; securely remove outdated copies.

recoveryRoadmap.description: A general checklist for family representatives after a death. The correct legal and tax process depends on whether the relevant jurisdiction is England, Wales, or Scotland.

meta.title: Family Recovery Roadmap - Great Britain
meta.reviewedBy: Official guidance reviewed; not a substitute for legal or tax advice

intro.condolence: We are sorry for your loss. This checklist is intended to help organise the first practical steps.
intro.howToUse: Confirm the jurisdiction and your authority first. Then secure records, notify the right organisations, and obtain professional advice where needed.

startHere: If there is an immediate safety or medical emergency, call 999 or 112.
Register the death and follow the registrar or coroner's instructions; timing and process differ between Scotland and England or Wales.
Ask the registrar whether Tell Us Once is available and obtain its reference if applicable. It does not notify all private providers.
Locate the will, identify the executor or appropriate representative, and confirm the correct jurisdiction before acting.
Secure identity, property, bank, insurance, pension, debt, and tax records. Keep a log of every organisation contacted.
Do not access accounts, distribute assets, or pay debts until authority and provider requirements have been checked.
legalFramework: England and Wales: probate and estate administration processes; see GOV.UK applying for probate.
Scotland: confirmation and Scottish estate administration processes; see the Scottish Courts and Tribunals Service.
Wills, succession, powers of attorney, tax, benefits, and property rules can differ by jurisdiction and individual circumstances.
Tell Us Once can notify specified government departments in England, Scotland, and Wales when eligibility requirements are met; private organisations may need separate notification.
Official guidance may change. Confirm all forms, eligibility, fees, and deadlines with the relevant authority or a qualified adviser.

phases.title: Immediate care and records
phases.focus: Follow official registration guidance, identify the responsible person, and protect important records.

keyActions.action: Follow the registrar, medical examiner, or coroner's instructions for registration and certificates.
keyActions.why: Registration and certificate processes are jurisdiction-specific and are needed for subsequent administration.

keyActions.action: Find the will and identify the named executor or other person entitled to deal with the estate.
keyActions.why: Only an authorised person should make estate decisions or contact providers as a representative.

keyActions.action: Secure the home, identity papers, will, financial records, devices, and any medicines or care information that need urgent attention.
keyActions.why: This protects property and helps representatives find the information needed for later steps.
keyActions.legalRef: General recordkeeping; seek advice for urgent legal questions

keyActions.action: Ask the registrar about Tell Us Once eligibility and keep the reference and any deadline supplied.
keyActions.why: The service can notify specified public bodies, but it does not replace contact with all private organisations.

mustHaveDocuments: National Insurance and NHS number records
Current bank, insurer, pension, and mortgage contacts

keyContacts.name: Relevant register office
keyContacts.use: Registration process and Tell Us Once reference

keyContacts.name: Existing or jurisdiction-appropriate solicitor
keyContacts.use: Will, authority, estate, and urgent legal questions

criticalMistakes: Assuming a relative can operate accounts without authority
Assuming the England and Wales probate process applies in Scotland
Sharing passwords or using another person's online banking
Assuming Tell Us Once contacts every organisation

phases.title: Notify providers and protect finances
phases.focus: Notify public bodies and private providers, understand immediate bills, and preserve a record of the estate.

keyActions.action: Use Tell Us Once if eligible; otherwise follow the relevant official process for notifying government departments.
keyActions.why: Benefits, tax, vehicle, and other public records may need updating, and the service has defined eligibility.

keyActions.action: Contact banks, mortgage providers, insurers, employers, utilities, and private pension schemes through their official bereavement channels.
keyActions.why: Tell Us Once does not notify all private institutions or personal pension schemes.

keyActions.action: Record assets, debts, regular payments, ownership, and provider responses; ask before stopping payments or moving funds.
keyActions.why: Joint ownership, contracts, and estate duties differ; assumptions can cause financial or legal problems.
keyActions.legalRef: Provider terms and jurisdiction-specific estate rules

keyActions.action: Contact pension providers or use the Pension Tracing Service if a scheme contact is unknown.
keyActions.why: The tracing service provides contact details, not confirmation that a pension exists or its value.

mustHaveDocuments: List of income, benefits, recurring payments, and debts
criticalMistakes: Assuming joint accounts or assets pass in the same way in every case
Paying debts from personal funds without checking responsibility
Overlooking private pension or employer benefits
Treating a provider reference as authority to operate an account

phases.title: Estate, tax, and property administration
phases.focus: Confirm the required authority, value the estate, and complete the appropriate tax and property processes.

keyActions.action: Ask the relevant institutions whether a grant is needed and obtain jurisdiction-specific advice on probate in England or Wales or confirmation in Scotland.
keyActions.why: The required process depends on the jurisdiction, assets, ownership, and provider requirements.

keyActions.action: Identify and value estate assets and liabilities; check HMRC guidance for inheritance tax and any reporting requirements.
keyActions.why: Tax reporting and payment requirements depend on estate facts and current rules.

keyActions.action: Keep complete records of decisions, valuations, expenses, provider correspondence, and distributions.
keyActions.why: Representatives may need to account to beneficiaries, creditors, HMRC, or a court.

keyActions.action: Check title, mortgage, insurance, and occupancy arrangements before selling, transferring, or changing property.
keyActions.why: Title, co-ownership, lender, and jurisdiction rules can affect what can be done and when.

mustHaveDocuments: Asset and debt inventory with valuation dates
Grant of probate or Scottish confirmation, if required
Property title, mortgage, and insurance records

keyContacts.name: HMRC inheritance tax and bereavement guidance
Qualified professional
keyContacts.use: Complex estate, tax, property, or cross-border advice

criticalMistakes: Distributing assets before checking authority, tax, and creditor requirements
Assuming a grant is always required or never required
Relying on old tax thresholds or deadlines

phases.title: Close out and review family plans
phases.focus: Complete provider matters and review the surviving household's records and arrangements.

keyActions.action: Confirm claims, final bills, account closures, pension decisions, and property records with each organisation.
keyActions.why: Each provider may have separate documentation, timelines, and confirmation requirements.

keyActions.action: Review the surviving household's will, powers of attorney, beneficiaries, insurance, and emergency contacts with qualified advisers where appropriate.
keyActions.why: Family circumstances and appointed roles may have changed.

keyActions.action: Update the family asset and digital-account inventory, keeping credentials in an appropriate password manager rather than this export.
keyActions.why: A current, safely stored index can reduce confusion during a future emergency.

mustHaveDocuments: Updated family document and digital-account index

keyContacts.name: Qualified adviser
keyContacts.use: Review household finances and protection needs

keyContacts.name: Qualified adviser for the relevant jurisdiction
keyContacts.use: Review wills, powers, and estate planning

criticalMistakes: Leaving outdated beneficiaries or representatives in place
Keeping credentials in an unprotected spreadsheet or PDF
Failing to retain copies of final provider correspondence

deathRegistration.action: Follow the registrar or coroner's instructions. Published registration timeframes differ between Scotland and England or Wales and may be affected by the circumstances.

tellUsOnce.scope: May be used for eligible deaths of people living in England, Scotland, or Wales; not for a person living in Northern Ireland or permanently abroad.
tellUsOnce.importantNote: It notifies specified public bodies, not every private organisation.

estateAuthority.englandAndWales: Check whether a grant of probate or letters of administration are required.
estateAuthority.scotland: Check the Scottish confirmation and estate administration process.

pensionTracing.service: The Pension Tracing Service can find contact details for a pension scheme; it cannot confirm whether a pension exists or its value.

glossary.definition: A person named in a will who may apply to deal with the estate, subject to the applicable jurisdiction and legal process.
An England and Wales legal document that can authorise an executor to deal with an estate; whether it is needed depends on the circumstances and institutions involved.
The Scottish court authority used by an executor to administer a deceased person's estate, where required.
An England and Wales legal arrangement. Scotland has separate continuing and welfare power-of-attorney arrangements.
A service for eligible people living in England, Scotland, or Wales to report a death to specified government organisations.
